name: Prize crossword No 23,945
preamble: Solve the clues and fit them into the grid wherever they will go, jigsaw-wise.

clue.text: See 1 down
Top soldier restricts setter's oversized house to thirty foot

indicators.note: to restrict is to hem in or confine, so one piece closes round the others

blocks.note: FM is a Field Marshal, the highest army rank
the setter has, from the setter's own mouth: I've
oversized as in overweight
HO is the standard abbreviation for house

explanation.surface: A general's grand house gets cut down to a modest thirty-foot plot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Setter's' is read as 'the setter has', giving I'VE. A fathom is six feet, so FIVE FATHOM is thirty feet, as in Ariel's song 'Full fathom five' in The Tempest.
explanation.definitionFit: Six feet make one fathom, so five of those nautical measures come to exactly thirty feet of depth.

clue.text: Passed being exhausted?

blocks.note: first meaning: having passed a test or round
second meaning: finished or used up

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests someone who passed out from exhaustion; the two words are separate senses of one adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both having qualified for the next stage and being completely finished or spent.

clue.text: Revisit row about brand

blocks.note: about as in 'argue over something'
a brand or kind of thing

explanation.surface: Going back to argue over a trade name again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Row' looks like a quarrel to go with 'about brand', but it belongs to the definition as a line of text.
explanation.definitionFit: To overtype is to key new characters on top of old ones, which is going back over a line of text.

clue.text: Fancy lines, past and high-level, get the bird

blocks.note: a fancy is a passing whim
British Rail, railway lines of the past, privatised in the 1990s
the El is an elevated, high-level railway, as in Chicago

explanation.surface: Fancy verses, old-fashioned and lofty, earn a hostile reception from the audience.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lines' does double duty: railway lines of the past (BR) and high-level ones (EL). 'Get the bird' sounds like being booed off stage.
explanation.definitionFit: The whimbrel is a wading bird, a smaller relative of the curlew with a curved bill.

clue.text: Pieces of brass neckerchief holder are deceptive

definitions.note: the answer is a verb meaning to deceive; the clue phrases it as a predicate

blocks.note: horns are brass instruments
a woggle is the ring holding a Scout's neckerchief

explanation.surface: Brass fittings on a Scout's scarf ring are not what they seem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pieces of brass' suggests metal parts, but means instruments of the brass section. A woggle is the leather or plastic ring Scouts use to fasten their neckerchief.
explanation.definitionFit: Hornswoggle is a jocular old American word for cheat, bamboozle or trick someone.

clue.text: Not much of a note

blocks.note: first meaning: tiny, pronounced my-NEWT
second meaning: a written memorandum, pronounced MIN-it

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as a short musical sound or a brief message; the two senses are pronounced differently.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective it means extremely small; as a noun it is a brief written record or memorandum.

clue.text: Balfour's pretty girl from Lancaster

blocks.note: first meaning: a pretty girl is a rose, here a named beauty in a literary allusion
second meaning: the heraldic badge of the House of Lancaster

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a girl from the town of Lancaster; the second sense is the emblem of the House of Lancaster in the Wars of the Roses, still the symbol of Lancashire.
explanation.definitionFit: A girl admired for her beauty is often called a rose, and the red flower was the Lancastrian badge in heraldry.

clue.text: Fifty poems to Geordieland form a magnet

blocks.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty
odes are lyric poems
taken as written
Geordies come from Tyneside, in the North East of England

explanation.surface: A batch of poems sent off to Newcastle become a draw for readers.
explanation.walkthrough: A Geordie is someone from Newcastle upon Tyne, in North East England, abbreviated NE.
explanation.definitionFit: Lodestone is naturally magnetised iron ore, the original natural magnet used in early compasses.

clue.text: Shakespearean sides

blocks.note: first meaning: the bumbling headborough who partners Dogberry in Much Ado About Nothing
second meaning: edges or borders, as of a road

explanation.walkthrough: The two words read like a description of characters in a play; the first is a character's name, the second a plain noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Grass edges beside a road are its verges, and the word means borders or margins generally.

clue.text: Great Italian painter judged mad sent back to patriarch

indicators.note: something sent back travels the way it came, so these letters run in the opposite direction

blocks.note: gran is Italian for great, as in Gran Turismo
Richard Dadd, Victorian painter declared insane after killing his father

explanation.surface: A great Italian artist, ruled insane, is packed off home to the head of the family.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Great Italian painter' wants to be a Renaissance master, but 'Great Italian' is only a word in Italian, and the painter is English: Richard Dadd spent his life in Bedlam and Broadmoor.
explanation.definitionFit: An old grandfather is the senior male of a family, the patriarch at the head of the clan.

clue.text: Next placings' effect is just - a pox on it

indicators.note: to effect something is to bring it about or produce it, so the letters are worked up into a new product

blocks.clueFragment: is just - a pox on it
blocks.note: the six words taken letter for letter, punctuation ignored

explanation.surface: A disgruntled competitor curses the way the next finishing places have been decided.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash and 'a pox on it' make it sound like a grumble about results, and 'placings' suggests a race; the fodder starts at 'is', which is easy to miss.
explanation.definitionFit: Juxtaposition is the act of setting things side by side, each item put next to its neighbour.

clue.text: Like Elizabeth Bennet's pride, with Julia and Crawford initially involved

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter of the word is kept
involved means tangled or intricate, so the letters are mixed up together

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
the opening letter of the surname

explanation.surface: Jane Austen talk: Elizabeth Bennet's pride, with characters from Mansfield Park mixed into the story.
explanation.walkthrough: Elizabeth Bennet is the heroine of Pride and Prejudice; Julia Bertram and the Crawfords are from Austen's Mansfield Park. The definition is 'Like Elizabeth Bennet's', completed in the mind by the other half of the title.
explanation.definitionFit: Elizabeth's failing in the novel is prejudice, so anything resembling hers is biased, showing preconceived judgement.

clue.text: One damn thing after another for a fellow whose forte may be who he is, in more than one manner of speaking

indicators.note: 'may be' says the word could take another form, so its letters are rearranged
one thing being inside another means it is held within it

blocks.note: taken as written
a chap is a man or fellow
taken as written

blocks.clueFragment: more than one manner of speaking
blocks.note: several ways of pronouncing a language
ID, identity, is who a person is

explanation.surface: A long-winded description of a talented man, whose speciality is being himself in many voices.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Forte' looks like a noun meaning strength, but its letters are the fodder for 'may be'. ID, short for identity, goes inside the accents.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom for a run of mishaps or misfortunes following closely one upon another.

clue.text: See 13 across
Report of crew missing money? There isn't any

indicators.note: a report is something heard, so we work with how the money's name is pronounced rather than spelt
missing means lacking, so the spoken word for the ship's team is dropped from the sound

blocks.note: the cruzeiro was the currency of Brazil, and said out loud it runs together two English words
taken as written: the sound to be dropped from the front

explanation.surface: A news item about sailors who have lost the ship's cash, ending with the grim admission that nothing is left.
explanation.walkthrough: CRUZEIRO, the old Brazilian currency, is pronounced 'crew zero'; take away the 'crew' sound and ZERO remains, which is just what missing money leaves you with.
explanation.definitionFit: Zero is the number naming nothing at all, so it fits the phrase saying no amount exists.

clue.text: Russian general greater than Gerald but lesser than Angelica

blocks.clueFragment: Russian general greater than Gerald but lesser than Angelica
blocks.note: surface reading: a ranking of three people by size or importance

blocks.clueFragment: greater than Gerald but lesser than Angelica
blocks.note: setter's reading: the spelling has one more letter than politician Gerald's surname and one fewer than painter Angelica's

explanation.surface: A Russian general is ranked above one person and below another.
explanation.walkthrough: Gerald Kaufman was a British Labour MP, one F and one N; Angelica Kauffmann was an 18th-century Swiss painter, two Fs and two Ns. The Tsarist general Konstantin von Kaufmann sits between with one F and two Ns.
explanation.definitionFit: Konstantin von Kaufmann was the Tsarist commander who governed Russian Turkestan in the 1860s and 1870s.

clue.text: Prize holding unknown painter

indicators.note: something holding another keeps it inside its grasp

blocks.note: a trophy cup is a prize
x, y and z are the unknowns of algebra

explanation.surface: An award goes to an artist nobody has heard of.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unknown painter' reads as one phrase, but 'unknown' is the algebraic letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Aelbert Cuyp was a Dutch Golden Age artist known for golden-lit landscapes with cattle.

clue.text: Wanted time with small boy

blocks.note: a year is a period of time
Ned, a short form of Edward

explanation.surface: Someone wished for a little time with their young son.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Small boy' means a short boy's name, a pet form of Edward, not a child.
explanation.definitionFit: To yearn is to long for or desire something intensely, so the past tense matches wished-for.

clue.text: Nick, American town student, get up!

blocks.note: burg is US slang for a town
L is the learner driver's plate
to arise is to get up

explanation.surface: Someone shouts at Nick, a student from a small American town, to get out of bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nick' looks like a name, but it is British slang for steal, the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To nick, in British slang, is to steal; breaking into a building to steal is to burgle it.

clue.text: No need to wait for this month?

definitions.note: a phrase describing something that needs no wait; the answer is an adjective

blocks.note: first meaning: immediate, like coffee made at once
second meaning: old business-letter usage, abbreviated 'inst.', for the current month

explanation.walkthrough: The question reads like impatience over a delivery date; the second sense is formal commercial jargon, as in 'your letter of the 5th inst.'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something immediate happens at once, with no delay, and old commercial correspondence used the word for the current month.

clue.text: Supplement to United Kingdom English twice revised

indicators.note: a revised text has been reworked, so the letters come out in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
the standard abbreviation
E for English, taken two times

explanation.surface: A supplement to a book on British English goes through two revisions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supplement' looks like a noun, an addendum, but is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To eke out a supply is to make it stretch further by adding to it bit by bit.

clue.text: Khaki fires land that's dreadfully soaked

indicators.note: dreadfully means terribly, badly done, so the letters are knocked out of order

blocks.note: the three words taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Soldiers in khaki fire on a sodden, waterlogged country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Soaked' suggests rain-drenched land, but it is slang for drank heavily, a past-tense verb like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To soak, informally, is to drink alcohol to excess, which the idiom about the fish expresses.

clue.text: Tobacco money

blocks.note: first meaning: a lump of tobacco for chewing
second meaning: British slang for a pound sterling

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as the cost of a smoking habit; the two words are separate senses of one short noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A plug of chewing tobacco is called this, and so, in British slang, is one pound sterling.

clue.text: No books on beast, first century, will be benign

blocks.note: taken as written
the New Testament, a set of books of the Bible
an ox is a beast of burden
I is the Roman numeral one, so first
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred

explanation.surface: With no books written about it yet, a first-century creature is considered harmless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First century' looks like a date, but splits into two Roman numerals, I and C. 'On' only places one piece next to another.
explanation.definitionFit: A benign substance or growth is harmless, causing no damage, as something without poison is.

clue.text: Return from fraud, an axed scheme for site of dome

indicators.note: taken from means drawn out of the wording that follows
to return is to go back the way you came, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: the run of letters straddling the three words

explanation.surface: Money is clawed back from a fraudulent, cancelled plan for a dome, like the Millennium Dome.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface recalls London's troubled Millennium Dome project. The dome of the answer is Coleridge's: 'In Xanadu did Kubla Khan / A stately pleasure-dome decree'.
explanation.definitionFit: Coleridge's poem Kubla Khan places the emperor's stately pleasure-dome in this legendary summer capital.

clue.text: Appointment in Yorkshire town not booked without hustle

indicators.note: 'not booked' says the abbreviation for book is struck out
one thing being inside another means it sits within it

blocks.note: a date is an appointment
Selby is a market town in North Yorkshire

explanation.surface: A meeting in a Yorkshire town was arranged without being booked in advance, in an unhurried way.
explanation.walkthrough: B is the abbreviation for book; dropping it from SELBY leaves SELY, which then holds DATE.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something calmly and unhurriedly, at a dignified pace, is the opposite of rushing about.

clue.text: Man's follower's change of heart is a reversal

indicators.note: the heart is the middle, so changing it rearranges only the central letters

blocks.note: undoing a knot reverses the tying

explanation.surface: A man's devoted disciple has a change of heart and turns against him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man' is short for Manchester, and the word that follows it in the football club's name is the answer. Swapping the middle two letters of UNTIED gives it.
explanation.definitionFit: Manchester United is the football club, so the word coming after Man in its name follows it.
